newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia to introduce ASX demutualisation bill.
newsitem.headline: Australia to introduce ASX demutualisation bill.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said on Thursday the government would soon introduce legislation that would enable the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) to demutualise.
Under the proposed legislation, individual shareholders would not be able to own more than five percent of the exchange's stock.

"The ASX is a special institution within the national economy and it would not be in the public interest for any one party to gain control of the ASX or carry significant influence over the governance of the ASX," Costello said in a statement.
Last October, ASX members approved the demutualisation plan in a move which would clear the way for the exchange to become the first publicly listed stock exchange in the world.
Costello said the government had agreed to allow the ASX to list on its own exchange with the listing to be supervised by the Australian Securities Commission (ASC).
"(This will) avoid any conflict of interest that supervision by the ASX of its own listing would create," Costello said.
He said demutualisation of the ASX would not alter regulation of the securities industry with the ASC retaining its watchdog role.
"Demutualisation of the ASX will ... confirm the status of the ASX as a leading securities market for the Asia-Pacific region," he said.
Costello said the exchange would also lose access to capital investment subsidies from the National Guarantee Fund (NGF) when it became a public company.

"Access to NGF moneys by A demutualised ASX, in circumstances where the profits from the capital investments funded by those moneys would pass to shareholders of the ASX, is no longer appropriate," he said.
The exchange currently has 522 individual members and 88 corporate members. The stock exchange members voted in favour of the demutualisation in October last year.
